To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the locally observed cosmic ray spectra can be understood as the superposition of a nearby (2-3  kpc) supernova source that was active two million years ago, and a much older (10-15  Myr) Galactic population.

the locally observed cosmic ray spectra of protons, antiprotons, and positrons are consistent with being produced by a nearby source that has injected approximately 10^{50}  erg in cosmic rays and was active approximately two millions years ago.
a nearby supernova that exploded approximately two million years in the past has injected cosmic ray protons, antiprotons, and positrons into the interstellar medium.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the local cosmic ray source which is responsible for the excess of antiparticles and for the change in slope of the spectrum of protons and heavier elements in the TeV energy range.
the signatures of a supernova in the cosmic ray spectrum.
the search for the signatures of a nearby supernova that occurred about 2 Myr ago in the cosmic ray spectrum.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

a supernova that exploded 2.5 million years ago is the most likely origin of the excess positrons and antiparticles in cosmic rays, and that it is the same supernova as the one that deposited ^{60} Fe isotopes on Earth.
the excesses of positrons, antiprotons and the spectral break of cosmic ray nuclei in the Tev-PeV energy are signatures of the same nearby supernova that has been detected by ^{60}Fe.
there is a supernova origin of the excess of antiprotons and positrons and a supernova origin for the local cosmic ray spectrum.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a nearby supernova has injected cosmic rays that are now observed on Earth as excess of positrons, antiprotons and the flattening of the proton spectrum.
a supernova event that occurred two million years ago is responsible for the observed excess of positrons, antiprotons, and the spectral break in the proton spectrum at ~10 ^{15.6}  eV.
a supernova explosion 2 million years ago, which is consistent with the ^{60}Fe data, can explain all the features of the cosmic ray spectrum.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cosmic ray observations can be used as a tool to study the recent history of our Galaxy.
the local cosmic rays have been produced by a nearby source, which is not part of the Galactic cosmic ray population.
the local cosmic rays are a unique laboratory for studying the physics of supernova explosions.
